indicators.name: Systolic blood pressure
indicators.howToMeasure: Seated, arm at heart level, after 5 minutes of rest. Use the onboard cuff before exercise.
indicators.whySpace: Microgravity shifts fluids toward the head and deconditions the heart and vessels. Blood pressure regulation changes in flight and after landing. Bands follow AHA categories: 120-129 (elevated) stays green, yellow starts at stage 1 hypertension (130), red at stage 2 (140) or hypotension (below 90).

actions.green: No action. Keep the daily routine.
actions.yellow: Repeat the measurement in 1 hour. Reduce salt, keep hydration and planned cardio exercise.
actions.red: Repeat now. If confirmed, report to the crew medical officer and log for the flight surgeon.

sources.title: AHA: Understanding blood pressure readings
NASA HRP: Risks of human spaceflight

indicators.name: Diastolic blood pressure
indicators.howToMeasure: Taken together with systolic pressure, same conditions.
indicators.whySpace: See systolic blood pressure: fluid shift and cardiovascular deconditioning.

actions.yellow: Repeat in 1 hour, review hydration and stress.
actions.red: Repeat now. If confirmed, report to the crew medical officer.

sources.title: AHA: Understanding blood pressure readings

indicators.name: Resting heart rate
indicators.howToMeasure: Right after waking, before getting out of the sleep station. Wearable, finger sensor or the camera pulse scan.
indicators.whySpace: A resting heart rate well above your own baseline can signal deconditioning, poor sleep, infection or stress.

actions.yellow: Check sleep and hydration. Re-measure tomorrow morning.
actions.red: Re-measure now. With symptoms (dizziness, chest pain) report to the crew medical officer immediately.

sources.title: AHA: All about heart rate (pulse); normal resting 60-100 bpm, trained athletes down to about 40
Royal College of Physicians 2017, National Early Warning Score (NEWS2): pulse <=40 and >=131 score 3, temperature <=35.0 score 3
Buchheit 2014, Monitoring training status with HR measures: typical day-to-day error of resting HR about 10%
NASA HRP: Risks of human spaceflight

indicators.name: Fasting blood glucose
indicators.howToMeasure: Finger-stick glucometer before breakfast, after at least 8 hours without food.
indicators.whySpace: Reduced physical load and stress hormones can change insulin sensitivity during long missions.

actions.yellow: Below 70: eat 15 g of fast carbohydrates and re-test in 15 minutes. 100-125: review diet and exercise adherence, re-test in 2 days.
actions.red: Below 54: eat 15 g of fast carbohydrates now, re-test in 15 minutes and tell a crewmate. 126 or above: re-test fasting and report.

sources.title: ADA: Diagnosis of diabetes and prediabetes
ADA 2024, Glycemic goals and hypoglycemia: level 1 below 70, level 2 below 54 mg/dL

indicators.name: Body temperature
indicators.howToMeasure: Oral or ear thermometer, at rest, not right after exercise.
indicators.whySpace: Spaceflight alters the immune response and can reactivate latent viruses. Fever is an early sign. Core body temperature of astronauts also rises by about 1 °C on long missions, so compare with your own in-flight baseline.

actions.red: Report to the crew medical officer. Limit contact with crewmates if infection is suspected.

sources.title: CDC: Definitions of signs and symptoms of ill travelers (fever: 38 °C / 100.4 °F or higher)
Brown et al. 2012, Accidental hypothermia (core temperature below 35 °C)
Obermeyer et al. 2017, Individual differences in normal body temperature: mean 36.6 °C, 95% range 35.7-37.3 °C
Royal College of Physicians 2017, National Early Warning Score (NEWS2): pulse <=40 and >=131 score 3, temperature <=35.0 score 3
Crucian et al. 2018, Immune system dysregulation during spaceflight
Stahn et al. 2017, Increased core body temperature in astronauts during long-duration space missions
NASA HRP: Risks of human spaceflight

indicators.name: Sleep
indicators.howToMeasure: Self-report or wearable: total sleep time last night.
indicators.whySpace: Shifted light-dark cycles, noise and workload cut sleep on missions. Sleep loss reduces alertness and performance.

actions.yellow: Keep a fixed sleep window, dim screens 1 hour before sleep.
actions.red: Two nights in a row: tell the commander, avoid critical tasks without a cross-check, run the PVT test.

sources.title: Watson et al. 2015, Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult (AASM/SRS)
Barger et al. 2014, Sleep deficiency in astronauts before, during and after spaceflight (ISS average about 6 h)
Van Dongen et al. 2003, The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness: 6 h or less per night for 14 days impairs like up to 2 nights without sleep

indicators.name: Mood
indicators.howToMeasure: Self-rating from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good), same time every day.
indicators.whySpace: Isolation and confinement are one of the five hazards of human spaceflight and affect behavioral health.

actions.yellow: Schedule a private call with family or a psychologist, plan leisure time.
actions.red: Several days in a row: talk to the crew medical officer and the ground behavioral health team.

sources.title: NASA: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight

indicators.name: Reaction time (PVT)
indicators.howToMeasure: 3-minute reaction test in the app. Same time of day each run.
indicators.whySpace: Slower reactions are an objective sign of fatigue or sleep loss, before you notice it yourself. Yellow starts when the average response reaches the 3-minute PVT-B lapse threshold (355 ms), red at the classic 10-minute PVT lapse threshold (500 ms).

actions.yellow: Postpone non-urgent precision tasks, take a short rest.
actions.red: Do not perform critical tasks alone. Report fatigue to the commander.

sources.title: Basner et al. 2015, Development and validation of the Cognition test battery for spaceflight
Basner, Mollicone, Dinges 2011, Validity and sensitivity of a brief PVT (PVT-B): lapse = 355 ms or slower
Basner, Dinges 2011, Maximizing sensitivity of the PVT to sleep loss: lapse = 500 ms or slower

indicators.name: Cumulative radiation dose
indicators.howToMeasure: Personal dosimeter reading, summed over the mission.
indicators.whySpace: NASA limits career effective dose to 600 mSv and requires doses as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). Yellow starts at half of the limit, red at 90% of it. Beyond Earth's magnetic field the daily dose rises several times.

actions.yellow: Minimize time in low-shielded modules, sleep in the shielded quarters.
actions.red: Close to the career limit: mission control must review EVA and activity plans.

sources.title: NASA OCHMO: Radiation protection technical brief, NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 [V1 4030] career limit below 600 mSv
CSA: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
